rv.q: No amount of charm — and Mr. Canada is charming — can make that dramaturgical device stop creaking.
Both plays dive deeply into the internal torments of their characters, whose painful journeys toward redemption are compelling if sometimes ponderous.

Frustratingly, what all three shows have in common is a feeling of paddedness, along with a well-intentioned but half-baked search for a gestural vocabulary beyond straight realism, the results of which haven’t so much cracked open the stories as burdened them with predictable devices.
The Ufot Cycle is one of the most ambitious and exciting dramatic works currently being crafted for the American stage.

A two-character play, In Old Age presents a predictable, well-worn, romantic tale that is given much-needed charm by Ron Canada’s exuberant presence as Abernathy and Chevannnes’ darling portrayal of the frail yet feisty Abasiama.

Unfortunately, runboyrun and In Old Age, the two now on display at New York Theatre Workshop, do not stand alone apart from the earlier plays and would be better served by being paired with other parts of the cycle.
At this point, however, the Ufot Cycle is starting to resemble a collection of puzzle pieces, not all of which belong to the same picture.
Unfortunately, despite superb acting and a game sense of "we-can-do-it" gumption, the plays, presented as one evening of work, are an unrelentingly slow, grim slog.
Missing Mfoniso Udofia’s plays is missing enormous opportunities for grappling with what it means to be human.
Since the excellent piece is presented first you could go and leave during intermission, a reversal of second acting.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Ufot Cycle double bill, with some finding both plays compelling explorations of a Nigerian-American family while others deem the pairing uneven—though they disagree on which half works better.
